Proposed: mirror `src/` with `test/kicad/draft/`, `test/agent/providers/`, `test/commands/`.

### 3.3 Smaller items

- `agent/filetools.ts` is the only unhyphenated compound among `bom-export`, `dock-renderer`, `live-prompt`, `tool-protocol`, `cli-args`, `response-cache`.
- `agent/types.ts` is 51 lines of tool-call types under a name promising all types, next to an existing `providers/tool-protocol.ts`.
- `commands/repl-inspect.ts` (353) is REPL slash-command helpers, not a command.
- `scripts/ui-demo.ts` is a mock session while `scripts/demo-simple.sh` is a real pipeline run, and both are called "demo".
- `agent-install-prompt.md` and `docs/src/content/docs/getting-started/agent-install.md` share 65 identical lines and will drift.

## Plan

Sequenced so the heavy moves land after `deterministic-schematic-drafting` archives, since a tree-wide rename conflicts with every open branch.

### Phase 1: dead weight, no code impact

- [ ] Remove `assets/copperhead-linkedin.{gif,mp4}` (1.06 MB, zero references)
- [ ] Decide on `copperhead-1080p.mp4` and `home-resonance.mp3` (2.2 MB, comment-only references); keep with a note in `scripts/demo-rename-1080p.tape` explaining they are manual-edit inputs, or drop them
- [ ] Remove `pipeline-run-logs/` (368 KB, zero references)
- [ ] Decide whether `manual-tests/reference-boards/*/reference/*.png` stay tracked (756 KB, regenerable, not part of the test contract)
- [ ] Archive the nine complete OpenSpec changes via `/opsx:archive`, merging delta specs into `openspec/specs/SPEC.md`
- [ ] Decide the fate of the four dormant changes: keep as backlog with a marker, or close
- [ ] Collapse `.claude/commands/opsx/` and `.claude/skills/openspec-*` to one surface
- [ ] Prune the 45 local branches already merged into main (83 total). Note: the `draft-engine-component-tests` worktree holds unmerged commit `54e85dd` and must be left alone

### Phase 2: low-risk renames, isolated importers

- [ ] `src/kicad/cli.ts` to `kicad-cli.ts`
- [ ] `src/openspec/cli.ts` to `openspec-cli.ts`
- [ ] `src/agent/filetools.ts` to `file-tools.ts`
- [ ] `src/commands/export.ts` to `export-bom.ts`
- [ ] `src/kicad/draft/draft.ts` to `draft/index.ts`
- [ ] Move `src/kicad/emit.ts` into `src/kicad/draft/`
- [ ] Rename `create-hardening` / `draft-hardening` / `toolcall-extra` tests to say what they cover
- [ ] `src/agent/types.ts` to `tool-types.ts`, or merge into `providers/tool-protocol.ts`

### Phase 3: structural, after `deterministic-schematic-drafting` archives

- [ ] Extract `src/tui/` from `src/agent/` and `src/util/`, absorbing `src/layout/`
- [ ] Split `src/kicad/` along the five concerns above
- [ ] Untangle BOM: `src/util/markdown-table.ts`, `src/bom/`, `commands/export-bom.ts`
- [ ] Move `src/commands/repl-inspect.ts` into `src/repl/`
- [ ] Restructure `test/` to mirror `src/`
- [ ] Consider splitting `src/kicad/draft/engine.ts` (1,637 lines)

## Effect on the invariants

No effect. Every item is a move, a rename, or a deletion of unreferenced files. Spec-gating of write tools and verification-gating of mutations are untouched. Phase 3 moves `legibility.ts` and `score.ts` consumers around but does not change when the verification gate fires.

The one thing to watch: Phase 1's OpenSpec archiving edits `openspec/specs/SPEC.md`, which is the source of truth, so it should be reviewed as a spec change rather than as hygiene.

issues.title: Post-merge review of #160/#202: verifier misreports engine-owned power symbols, IR power parts are silently dropped, and a stale symbol-dir env var disables search
issues.body:
## What happened

Post-merge review of the `deterministic-schematic-drafting` surface (#160 and #202, both landed as merge commit `8b92152`) turned up three defects that survive on `main` at `c208680`. All three are reproduced below against committed fixtures, no live LLM involved.

Two of them share a root cause worth stating up front: **the symbol verifier and the drafting engine disagree about who owns power symbols.** The engine replaces power nets with its own generated `copperhead_power:*` symbols vendored into the project's `sym-lib-cache/`, but `verifySchematicSymbols` only ever searches installed system directories, and the engine silently discards any `power:*` part the model puts in the IR. The agent is therefore told to fix symbols that are correct, and gets no signal at all about symbols it asked for and did not get.

### 1. `verify_symbols` reports the engine's own power symbols as `wrong-library`

`verifySchematicSymbols` (src/kicad/symlib.ts) resolves lib_ids against `symbolSearchDirs()` only. It has no notion of the project's vendored `sym-lib-cache/`, so every `copperhead_power:*` symbol the engine generated fails to resolve, then fuzzy-matches its way to a stock lib_id.

On the committed `ldo-demo` reference board this yields four bogus findings out of six parts. Three are reported as `wrong-library` with a confident "use X instead" instruction, and the fourth as `no-library`:

```
checked 5 skipped 1
wrong-library | copperhead_power:3V3       -> "use Converter_DCDC:JTD1524S3V3 or Diode:BZV55B3V3 or Power_Protection:D3V3X8U9LP3810 or power:+3V3 instead"
wrong-library | copperhead_power:GND       -> "use power:GND or Device:Crystal_GND2 instead"
wrong-library | copperhead_power:PWR_FLAG  -> "use power:PWR_FLAG instead"
no-library    | copperhead_power:VIN       -> "library ... is not installed on this machine; cannot verify its pins"
```

Every one of these is wrong: the symbols exist and are correct, in `manual-tests/reference-boards/ldo-demo/sym-lib-cache/copperhead_power.kicad_sym`. `3V3` matching to a DC-DC converter and a Zener diode shows how far the fuzzy fallback reaches once resolution fails.

This is worse than noise, because the suggested fix is unreachable. The agent cannot act on it: the IR exposes no lever for power symbol lib_ids, and `edit_file` is refused on engine-drafted sheets. So stage 4 hands the model four "issues to reconcile" that have no legal resolution. That is the same shape as the deadlock in #163.

`symbolAvailabilityFacts` already knows to skip the `copperhead_power` namespace; this path does not. Fix is either to teach `symbolSearchDirs`/`verifySchematicSymbols` about the project cache, or to skip the engine-owned namespace the way the availability path does. The first is better: it also makes verification work for any vendored library, not just power.

### 2. Power parts in the IR are accepted, then silently dropped

`validateIntent` accepts an IR part whose symbol resolves with `isPower`, but the engine filters those parts out of every placement path (`src/kicad/draft/engine.ts`, the `!symbols.get(p.ref)!.isPower` guards around group naming, label extents, and placement). The part is never placed, never added to `lib_symbols`, never given a net endpoint, and never mentioned in the report.

Repro: take the committed `ldo-demo` intent, add one power part, and draft it.

```json
{ "ref": "PG1", "libId": "power:GND", "value": "GND", "footprint": "", "group": "Indicator" }
```
with `"PG1.1"` appended to the `GND` net's pins.

```
ok=true | PG1 present in sheet? false | power:GND placed? false
notes: []
groups: [{"name":"Indicator","members":["D1","R1"]},{"name":"Power","members":["C1","C2","J1","U1"]}]
vendoredLibIds includes power:GND? true
```

The draft reports success. `PG1` appears nowhere in the emitted sheet, it is absent from its own group's member list, and `notes` is empty. The engine even vendors `power:GND` into `sym-lib-cache/` on the way past, so the project accumulates a cached symbol for a part that was never drawn.

Dropping the part is arguably the right behavior, since the engine synthesizes its own per-pin power symbols and a model-authored one would be redundant. The bug is that it happens silently. A model that writes `power:GND` into the IR, sees `ok: true`, and finds no note has no way to learn that its mental model is wrong, so it will keep doing it. Either reject it in `validateIntent` with a finding that names the correct approach, or place it, or at minimum emit a note.

### 3. A stale `KICAD*_SYMBOL_DIR` disables symbol search entirely

`symbolSearchDirs` (src/kicad/symlib.ts) treats an env override as exclusive, which is intentional and documented in the comment above it: a caller pinning an isolated directory should not get the machine's stock install appended. But the exclusivity test is `fromEnv.length` measured **after** the entries are filtered for existence, not on whether the variable was set. So a variable pointing at a directory that no longer exists collapses the search path to nothing instead of falling back:

```
no env    -> 1 dirs  ['/usr/share/kicad/symbols']
stale env -> 0 dirs  []
```

With zero search dirs, every symbol tool reports "not installed on this machine" for every part, which is a false environmental claim rather than an empty result. That is a plausible mechanism behind the fabricated "reduced symbol library" constraint in #197, and it would make `search_symbols` (#200) and near-miss candidates (#195) fail the same way.

Note this one predates both PRs: it traces to `7140262`, so it is not a regression from the drafting work. It surfaced during this review.

The fix should preserve the documented exclusivity, so it needs to distinguish "set" from "set and resolvable". Failing loudly when an override is set but resolves to nothing seems better than either silently falling back or silently searching nothing.

## Steps to reproduce

All three run offline against committed fixtures. Findings 1 and 3 need no scratch setup:

```ts
import { symbolSearchDirs, verifySchematicSymbols } from './src/kicad/symlib.js';

// Finding 3
await symbolSearchDirs({});                                          // -> ['/usr/share/kicad/symbols']
await symbolSearchDirs({ KICAD_SYMBOL_DIR: '/nonexistent/stale' });   // -> []

// Finding 1
await verifySchematicSymbols('manual-tests/reference-boards/ldo-demo/reference/ldo-demo.kicad_sch');
```

Finding 2: copy `manual-tests/reference-boards/ldo-demo/schematic.intent.json` into a scratch repo, add the `PG1` part and net pin shown above, then call `draftSchematicToText({ repoRoot, schematic: 'reference/ldo.kicad_sch', today: '2026-08-08' })`.

## Which command

create (stage 4 drafting and symbol verification), plus `check` for finding 3.

## Model backend

Not applicable. All three reproduce offline with no provider configured.

## Version and environment

copperhead 0.9.0 at `c208680`; node v24.18.0, kicad-cli 10.0.4, Pop!_OS 22.04 LTS.

## Related

- #204 (router net merge), found in the same review pass, already fixed by #205.
- #163: finding 1 produces the same unresolvable-gate shape.
- #197, #200, #195: finding 3 is a candidate mechanism for the false "library not installed" claims.
- #61: closed, but the same power-symbol-namespace assumption.

issues.title: Symbol ref/value slot selection ignores wires, foreign bodies, and existing text — 8 unfixable legibility errors blocked an ERC-clean stage
issues.body:
## Observed

lemondrop attempt-07 (`run-logs/2026-08-07T17-52-03/attempt-07`, main @ 2201e24) reached ERC-clean, drift-clean, netlist-correct — and the supervisor had to abort on 8 error-severity legibility findings the agent empirically proved immovable: across 8 drafts and 4 group configurations (finding counts 8/8/8/9/20) the residual set reproduced identically, because they are symbol-field placements the IR has no lever over:

- C9 Reference and Value overlap U1's body (the chain-lifted cap sits beside the MCU; its text lands on the neighbour)
- D4 Reference/Value sit on the DP wire (also colliding with the DP label)
- U8 Value sits on a wire at the same point as the MIDI_OUT_BUF label
- one power-symbol Value sits on a wire

## Root cause

`emitSymbols` slot selection (engine.ts, "member symbols with collision-free text slots") is a three-case heuristic that consults nothing: not wires, not neighbouring bodies, not already-placed text. The obstacle machinery (`centeredTextBox`, `segHitsBox`, `textObstacles`) is built immediately AFTER the slots are frozen, for the benefit of the label pass only. The power-pass value ride handles text-vs-text but not text-on-wire.

## Fix sketch

Keep the current heuristic as slot 1 (byte-stable goldens where it is already clean), then walk a deterministic slot ladder (below, above, right, left, then a second ring) testing the ref+value pair's boxes against wires (`segHitsBox`), foreign bodies, and text placed so far; first clear slot wins; fall back to the heuristic when nothing clears so the checker still reports honestly. Extend the power-pass value ride condition to include wire hits. Validate against the attempt-07 IR (preserved in the workspace stash `copperhead failed run 2026-08-08T09-21-53-709Z`): the drafted sheet should drop from 8 error findings to 0 or near it.

This is the last blocker class between the campaign and its first stage-4 commit: the electrical design is done and verified; only engine-owned text placement stands.

issues.title: Checkpoint-commit accepted drafts during stage 4, then repair on top — users get output continuously and rollback stops destroying work
issues.body:
## Why

Stage 4 is all-or-nothing today: the stage commits only when ERC + drift + legibility are all clean, and a failed attempt rolls the tree back (stash + clean). The lemondrop campaign (`run-logs/2026-08-07T17-52-03`) shows the cost: attempt-05 drafted the full 160-part sheet, was ERC-clean at one point, found and fixed two genuine electrical bugs — and the repo ended the day empty. The work survived only in a git stash (tracked files) while the agent's untracked handoff doc was destroyed outright. Retries restarted from zero, twice. The harness tracks this class as R6/I16/R9.

## Proposal

Commit an initial draft as soon as one is accepted, then let the repair loop commit on top:

1. **Flagged WIP checkpoints on the branch**: after each accepted `draft_schematic` (and each stage-attempt boundary), commit with an unmistakable marker, e.g. `copperhead: WIP schematic draft — ERC FAILING, 4 findings, NOT FOR FABRICATION`. The existing stage-complete commit remains the only certification. Rollback becomes reset-to-last-checkpoint instead of stash-and-clean, so a retry starts from the best known state by construction and the retry boundary can no longer discard the artifacts it exists to preserve.
2. Alternative, more conservative: a **parallel WIP ref** (`refs/copperhead/wip/<stage>`) so the main branch stays certified-only while every accepted draft is still committed, visible, and diffable.

## Invariant analysis

Verification-gated-out ("every mutation ends ERC-clean or rolls back") exists so the repo never holds an uncertified schematic mistakable for approved output. Option 1 preserves the guarantee by moving the certification claim from "it is in git" to "the stage-complete commit exists" — which the pipeline and harness already distinguish (`definition_of_done.every_stage_committed`) — with the WIP marker making status unmistakable to humans and tools. Option 2 preserves it verbatim. Either is a spec-level change to the rollback contract and should go through an OpenSpec proposal.

## What users gain

A reviewable KiCad sheet minutes into stage 4 instead of only at stage completion, monotonic progress across retries, and an end to the class of loss where hours of accepted work exist only in a stash (or, for untracked files, nowhere).

issues.title: Hierarchical schematics: emit one child sheet per SUBSYSTEMS group, draft and validate sheet-by-sheet
issues.body:
## Why

A 160-part flat sheet (lemondrop, `run-logs/2026-08-07T17-52-03`) spends most of its stage-4 iteration on density: paper-size escalation chasing text collisions, whole-sheet re-emission (~40k tokens of IR) to fix one group, whole-sheet blast radius when a late edit regresses, and a router working around every other group's stub columns (the I22/#204 class shrinks with fewer foreign columns per sheet). Past ~200 parts a flat sheet also stops being reviewable by a human at all.

## Why it is cheaper than it looks

The IR already carries the hierarchy semantically, unchanged:

- every part names a `group` (a SUBSYSTEMS.md heading) — that is the child-sheet assignment;
- the engine already distinguishes in-group nets from cross-group nets (drawn today as "net labels between groups") — cross-group nets are exactly the hierarchical labels / sheet pins;
- a top sheet is derivable: one sheet symbol per group, pins from the cross-group net set, plus the title block.

## Sketch

1. Emitter: one `<project>-<group>.kicad_sch` per group plus an auto-generated top sheet; same deterministic byte-stable emission per file.
2. Stage 4 becomes a per-sheet loop: draft, validate, and repair ONE ~20-part sheet at a time — bounded context per turn, findings scoped to a sheet, each clean sheet separately committable, and a regression in one sheet cannot discard another (the structural fix for the lost-work problem the harness tracks as R6/I16).
3. Gates: legibility/score/wire-contact per sheet; ERC once across the hierarchy (kicad-cli handles hierarchical designs natively); drift checker learns sheet-qualified paths.
4. Scope honesty: this touches the drafting standard at spec level (single-sheet group boxes are pinned in the AC-16 contracts), the golden corpus, and every gate — an OpenSpec proposal, not a fix. Recent campaign evidence (attempt-05 reaching ERC-clean on a flat A1 with 4 cosmetic findings) says flat sheets are not the current blocker, so this is sequenced after the first end-to-end green run.

issues.title: Stage-4 entry knows which BOM parts are unresolvable — offer them to the human instead of spending agent turns
issues.body:
## Observed

The stage-4 pin dossier (PR #202) deterministically resolves every BOM part before the first agent turn, so at that moment the pipeline already knows the complete list of parts with NO INSTALLED SYMBOL. Today that list is handed to the agent, which then spends turns negotiating functional substitutes: on the lemondrop brief, attempt-02 spent ~12 turns swapping the same three parts (TLV320AIC3204, TLP2361, PESD5V0X2UAT) that attempt-05 later paid to re-derive, at hundreds of thousands of tokens per stage-attempt.

Choosing a substitute part is a decision a human makes in seconds from the candidate list; the expensive agent work that should remain is the follow-through (pin map, datasheet consequences), not the deliberation.

## Proposal

When the dossier finds unresolvable parts at schematic-stage entry:

1. **`--interactive`**: pause before the first agent turn with the absence list and each part's nearest candidates, and let the human edit `docs/BOM.md` or approve a substitution before any tokens are spent.
2. **Autonomous runs**: a config knob (`unresolvableParts: 'agent' | 'stop'`, default `'agent'` to preserve run-to-completion semantics) where `'stop'` fails fast with a structured report naming the parts and candidates, so the human fixes the BOM and resumes at one stage's cost instead of funding an in-run negotiation.

Scope note: stage 3's `search_symbols` requirement already prevents fresh BOMs from reaching stage 4 with absences; this checkpoint is the cheap exit for legacy or resumed workspaces where the BOM predates that rule.

Evidence: `copperhead-test-harness/run-logs/2026-08-07T17-52-03/` attempts 02 and 05 (substitution negotiation transcripts), and the dossier absence lines in attempt-06's `create.log`.

issues.title: Deterministic router merges two distinct nets (multiple_net_names): HSE_DRV shorted to TOUCH_IRQ survives every intent-level lever
issues.body:
## Observed

Harness run lemondrop attempt-05 (`copperhead-test-harness/run-logs/2026-08-07T17-52-03/attempt-05`, branch `feat/symbol-pin-dossier` @ `a2ba5f5`, 160-part STM32H7 granular synth). Stage 4 drafted a full netlist (160 parts, ~108 nets, 513 wire segments, 248 labels, 62 no-connects, nine group boxes; `verify_symbols` clean, `check_drift` clean) and ERC consistently failed with exactly one electrical error:

```
multiple_net_names: Both HSE_DRV and TOUCH_IRQ are attached to the same items
```

tying U3.13 (PH1, 24.576 MHz crystal drive via R6) to the TOUCH_IRQ net (U3.97/PE0, J8.12, R44). Shipping it would push a netlist into layout with the HSE drive shorted to the touch interrupt.

## Why this looks like an engine routing artifact, not an intent error

The stage-4 agent tested and disproved four repair hypotheses, methodically, before refusing to certify (its full write-up is preserved in the failed-run stash `copperhead failed run 2026-08-07T23-34-46-178Z` in the workspace, file `docs/STAGE4-STATUS.md`):

1. Net rename: the collision reproduced verbatim under different names.
2. Sheet size: reproduced on A2, A1, and A0.
3. Group ordering: five `hints.groupOrder` permutations plus the engine default.
4. Part declaration order: byte-identical output coordinates, so declaration order does not affect placement at all.

The intent JSON names two disjoint nets; the drafted geometry connects them. A wire segment routed by the engine appears to make contact with both nets' items, which KiCad then reports as one net carrying two names.

Relation to I2 (`fix e5c4f34`): that work made net-merge a hard ERC failure, and the gate held here (the run refused rather than certifying). This issue is the generative half: the router can still produce the merged geometry the gate exists to catch.

## Cheapest known unblock

The agent's proposed topology workaround: drop R6 (a 0 ohm placeholder in the crystal drive) and wire Y1 direct, removing the pass-through the router routes badly. That unblocks the brief; the engine defect remains.

## Repro material

- Constraint recorded by the run: `mcu.hse_drv_touch_irq_net_merge`
- Evidence: `run-logs/2026-08-07T17-52-03/attempt-05/evidence/` transcripts (three stage-attempts; the third contains the four-hypothesis search), plus the stashed IR that reproduces the merge deterministically.

issues.title: Stage 4 spends most of its turns reconstructing pin tables the machine already has
issues.body:
## Observed

Two harness runs of the lemondrop brief (`copperhead-test-harness/run-logs/2026-08-07T17-52-03`, STM32H743 granular synth, 158 refdes), both on the #198 build:

- **attempt-04, stage-attempt 1** (the furthest any stage-4 run has gotten): of the 19 turns to an accepted draft, roughly turns 3–18 — about 10 of 15 minutes — went to recovering pin names, largely via `read_file` over raw `.kicad_sym` spans. The transcript shows the agent paging through polyline geometry (`(xy -3.81 1.27) …`) hunting for `(pin …)` nodes for BAV99, TPS61165, 6N137, SS34.
- **attempt-02, stage-attempt 2** found a different route to the same data: a "probe draft" containing only unproven parts, each with one deliberately bogus pin, so a single validation report would echo back every real pin list ("Small IR containing only the parts whose lib_id or pin names are still unproven … each with a bogus pin, so one report returns every real pin list").

Both are workarounds for the same gap: the agent must author `REF.PIN` net endpoints from real library pin numbers, but nothing hands it a pin table. The stage prompt's own oracle is reactive ("validation lists a part's actual pins when you name one that does not exist") — pins are learned one failed guess at a time, or by reading sexp files never meant for that.

## Why it's cheap to fix

Everything needed already exists:

- `resolveLibrarySymbol` (src/kicad/symlib.ts) resolves a lib_id to its real pins, following `extends` links.
- `pinsOfSymbolNode` extracts number/name/electrical type.
- `searchInstalledSymbols` (#198) maps a part name to ranked lib_id candidates.
- `symbolAvailabilityFacts` (#198 + review follow-ups) is the established pattern for a capped, coverage-disclosed machine-fact block injected into a prompt.

And the BOM is frozen before stage 4 starts, so the part list is known at stage entry.

## Proposal

1. **Pin dossier at stage-4 entry**: before the first agent turn, resolve every BOM part (MPN, falling back to Value) to its installed-symbol candidates and inject a compact block into the stage prompt: top lib_id per part, pin table (number=name/type), and a MULTI-UNIT flag where the drafting engine would refuse the symbol (the SN74LVC2G17 trap from attempt-02). Capped by size with the overflow named, never silently truncated — same contract as `symbolAvailabilityFacts`.
2. **`symbol_pins` tool**: takes a lib_id, returns the resolved pin table; on a miss, ranked candidates in that library plus cross-library hits. Covers parts the agent swaps mid-stage, when the entry dossier is stale. Read-only, no unlock.

Expected effect: the ~15 discovery turns collapse into zero for dossier-covered parts; the bogus-pin probe pattern loses its reason to exist; first draft call moves from turn ~19 to roughly turn 2–3.

Evidence transcripts: `run-logs/2026-08-07T17-52-03/attempt-04/evidence/2026-08-07T20-26-54-462Z/transcript.jsonl` (read_file geometry paging), `attempt-02/evidence/2026-08-07T16-33-02-143Z/transcript.jsonl` (bogus-pin probe). Tracked harness-side as R14.

issues.title: search_symbols presents approximate matches as availability: ESP32-C3-MINI-1 resolves to the bare ESP32-C3 SoC, while STM32F103C8T6 resolves to nothing
issues.body:
Follow-up from the review of #198 (branch `fix/symbol-candidate-quality`, not yet merged). The ranking fix in that PR is correct; this is about what the tool *renders*, and it reintroduces the wrong-part outcome #196 was opened to prevent, one layer up.

## The mechanism

`rankSymbolNames` ([src/kicad/symlib.ts](src/kicad/symlib.ts)) sorts candidates into four tiers: 0 exact (separator-insensitive), 1 prefix, 2 substring, 3 name-inside-query (`c.length >= 3 && q.includes(c)`). `searchInstalledSymbols` now ranks these globally, which is right. But the `search_symbols` handler ([src/agent/tools.ts](src/agent/tools.ts)) discards the tier and prints one flat list:

```
installed symbols matching "<query>":
  - Lib:Name
  - Lib:Name
```

The tool description promises "exact matches first" without saying where exact stops, so a tier-3 near-miss is typographically indistinguishable from a tier-0 hit. Stage 3's prompt ([src/commands/create.ts](src/commands/create.ts)) then tells the agent that a part is drawable if its symbol appears here, and to substitute any part that has none. A single approximate result therefore reads as "verified available".

## Reproduction

Against the stock KiCad symbol set on a normal Linux install (222 libraries in `/usr/share/kicad/symbols`), using the PR branch:

| Query | Returned | Reality |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ESP32-C3-MINI-1` | `MCU_Espressif:ESP32-C3` (only result) | Wrong part. The query is a shielded SMD module with an integrated antenna; `ESP32-C3` is the bare QFN32 SoC, pin 1 `LNA_IN`. Different footprint, different pinout, not substitutable. |
| `AudioJack3_Ground_Switch` | exact hit, then `AudioJack3_Ground_SwitchTR`, `Simulation_SPICE:SWITCH`, `AudioJack3`, `AudioJack3_Ground` | Correct hit is first, but four differently-pinned parts follow it with nothing marking them as approximate. `Simulation_SPICE:SWITCH` is not a connector at all. |
| `STM32F103C8T6` | *(nothing)* | False negative. `MCU_ST_STM32F1:STM32F103C8Tx` is installed; KiCad's `x` package wildcard is not a substring of the full orderable MPN, so no tier matches. |

`ESP32-C3-MINI-1` is not a hypothetical: it is the exact part from #196's sensor-node evidence, where stage 3 committed it and stage 4 had nowhere legal to go. With this tool in place, stage 3 now gets an answer, and the answer points at the wrong silicon.

## Why it matters more than an unhelpful result

The two rows fail in opposite directions and compound. The false negative pushes the agent to substitute a part it did not need to substitute, and the false positive gives it a confident-looking target to substitute *toward*. The resulting BOM row passes stage 3, and the wrong-pinout symbol can pass ERC in stage 4 while being electrically wrong on the real board, which is the failure class the `verify_symbols` docstring already calls out for hand-authored `lib_symbols`.

## Suggested

Label match strength rather than filter it. Approximate hits are genuinely useful (`TPS61165` finding `Driver_LED:TPS61165DBV` is a tier-1 prefix hit and is the whole point of #196), so the fix is to stop presenting them as equivalent:

- Group the handler output into exact matches and approximate ones, and state plainly in the approximate section that these are different parts requiring confirmation before a BOM row is written.
- Return the tier alongside the lib_id so callers other than the prompt can act on it.
- Separately, teach matching about KiCad's package-suffix wildcard (`STM32F103C8Tx` for `STM32F103C8T6`), which closes the false negative without loosening anything.

Deliberately **not** suggested: a stage-3 completion gate that refuses a BOM row whose part has no installed symbol. That was floated in #196, and the table above is the argument against building it on today's matching: it would have refused a valid `STM32F103C8T6` row outright. The gate only becomes safe once MPN-to-symbol resolution handles package wildcards and reports its own confidence. #198's `create-pipeline` delta records this reasoning.

Related: #195 (candidate ranking), #196 (availability checked too late), #197 (refusals fact-checked), #185 (cross-library search).

issues.title: Recovery supervisor accepts a refusal's environmental claims unverified: a fabricated 'reduced symbol library' constraint aborted a run on a machine with the full stock set
issues.body:
Lemondrop harness run (`copperhead-test-harness/run-logs/2026-08-07T17-52-03/attempt-01/`, stage 4, `claude-code`, branch `fix/spec-budget-dual-write-reconciliation` @ da3325c).

## What happened

The stage-4 agent probed `draft_schematic` five times. Probe 3 used truncated lib_ids (`Audio:TLV320`, `Isolator:TLP`) and the validator answered with genuine in-library candidates — `closest: TLV320AIC23BPW, …` and `closest: TLP127, TLP130, TLP131, …` — proving both libraries exist and are readable. The agent probed **none** of the returned candidates (its follow-ups were names from its own head: `TLV320AIC3254`, `TLV320AIC3105`, `TLP2309`, `TLP2361_Logic`), then recorded via `record_constraint`, as "VERIFIED ABSENT", that "the Audio and Isolator libraries [are] entirely" missing and that "every suggestion probed (… TLV320AIC23BPW … TLP127 …) does not exist". `Audio:TLV320AIC23BPW` resolves on this machine.

The recovery supervisor then consumed the fabricated constraint at face value — diagnosis: "an environmental gap no retry can fix" — and aborted the stage with two of its three attempts unused. The machine has the full 222-library stock KiCad 10.0.4 package; 4 of the 6 refused subsystem blocks were drawable under correctly-spelled installed names (see #195, #185).

## Why this is a supervisor defect and not just an agent one

This is the fifth agent-fabrication sighting in the harness logs, but the first where the false facts left narration: `record_constraint` made them doc-truth, and the supervisor's abort decision quotes them. A transcript cross-check of claimed-vs-actual tool calls would not catch this variant — every tool call really ran; the false part is the *coverage claim* ("every suggestion probed"). The one thing that catches it is re-checking the claim against the machine.

## Suggested

Before accepting a refusal (or abort recommendation) whose stated blocker is symbol availability, run one deterministic re-probe of the refusal's named lib_ids — a single `draft_schematic` validation call, no LLM. If any cited-absent lib_id resolves, or the cited library yields candidates, the refusal's premise is false: classify the attempt as `unverified-refusal` (retry with the contradiction injected) instead of an environmental abort. Symbol availability is a machine fact; no refusal that turns on it should be adjudicated from prose.

issues.title: Part selection commits BOM lib_ids the installed libraries cannot resolve; the first existence check runs three stages later
issues.body:
Reproduced on three of the last four harness briefs (evidence dirs in `copperhead-test-harness/run-logs/`):

- **sensor-node** (`2026-08-04T02-40-30/attempt-01`): stage 3 committed `RF_Module:ESP32-C3-MINI-1`, `Sensor_Gas:SGP40`, `Sensor_Humidity:SHT41-AD1B` — none installed. 44/46 parts of the stage-4 IR validated and the stage still had nowhere legal to go.
- **bench-psu** (`2026-08-04T02-40-37/attempt-01`): INA301A2 selected as the load-bearing current-limit comparator; no INA301 symbol exists in the installed set.
- **lemondrop** (`2026-08-07T17-52-03/attempt-01`): U5 `TLV320AIC3204`, U7 `TLP2361`, D6/D7 `PESD5V0X2UAT` — all absent (installed `Audio` tops out at TLV320AIC23B*/3100; `Isolator` has TLP2310/2761/2770; only PESD5V0L*/S1UL variants ship). All three had same-library substitutes (`TLV320AIC3100`, `TLP2310`, `PESD5V0L4UF`) that stage 3 could have picked had anything checked.

The model picks these parts because it knows them from training data, and nothing in the stage-2/3 prompts or gates says "the design must be capturable with the libraries on this machine". By the time `draft_schematic` runs the first deterministic lib_id check inside stage 4, the GPIO map and BOM are committed doc-truth, so the stage-4 agent's refusal logic is locally sound — substituting a different-package symbol under a committed pin map mis-assigns pins while passing ERC. The brief becomes unwinnable at stage 4 no matter how well the IR is authored.

Symbol availability is a machine fact checkable in milliseconds, not a judgement call. Related: #133 documents that stages 1–3 have no deterministic verification at all, and that `verify_symbols` is advisory where it does run.

**Suggested:** expose the existing resolver (`resolveLibrarySymbol`, `src/kicad/symlib.ts`) to stage 3 — either as a tool the agent must run over the BOM before finishing, or as a stage-exit gate that refuses to commit a BOM row whose lib_id does not resolve, printing the same candidates the stage-4 validator prints (with #185's cross-library search, those candidates become actionable). The mismatch then surfaces while part choice is still cheap to change.

issues.title: Symbol near-miss candidates are polluted by sub-unit entries and miss separator-variant names (Device:Rotary_Encoder → closest: C, D, R)
issues.body:
Found driving `copperhead create` end-to-end on a granular-synth brief (harness evidence: `copperhead-test-harness/run-logs/2026-08-07T17-52-03/attempt-01/`, stage 4, branch `fix/spec-budget-dual-write-reconciliation` @ da3325c). Two defects in the near-miss candidate lists that `draft_schematic` prints on a `no-symbol` finding, distinct from and compounding #185 (no cross-library search):

## 1. Fuzzy matching misses separator variants and returns garbage instead

Probing `Device:Rotary_Encoder` returned:

```
SW3: "Device:Rotary_Encoder" does not exist in the library — closest: C, D, R
```

`Device:RotaryEncoder_Switch` (plus `RotaryEncoder`, `RotaryEncoder_Switch_MP`) sits in that very library, one underscore away from the query. The matcher missed it and instead proposed three single-letter generic passives — worse than no suggestion, because it reads as "this library holds nothing like your part". The same run missed `Connector:Micro_SD_Card*` for the query `Connector:microSD_Card` (case + underscore placement).

Candidate matching should compare names case-insensitively with separators (`_`, `-`) stripped, so `Rotary_Encoder` ↔ `RotaryEncoder_Switch` and `microSD_Card` ↔ `Micro_SD_Card` rank as near-misses, and single-character symbols should never outrank multi-character prefix/substring matches for a multi-character query.

## 2. Sub-unit entries dilute the candidate list

Probing `Audio:TLV320` returned:

```
closest: TLV320AIC23BPW, TLV320AIC23BPW_0_1, TLV320AIC23BPW_1_1, TLV320AIC23BRHD, TLV320AIC23BRHD_0_1, TLV320AIC23BRHD_1_1, TLV320AIC23BxQE, TLV320AIC23BxQE_0_1
```

An 8-slot list carrying 3 real placeable symbols. `<name>_<unit>_<style>` sub-symbols are internal structure, not placeable candidates, and should be filtered before ranking.

## Why it matters

In this run the two facets fed a full stage-4 refusal and a supervisor abort: the agent concluded from these dead-end candidate lists that the machine's symbol library is "reduced" — on a box with the full 222-library stock set installed. Four of the six refused subsystem blocks were drawable under correctly-spelled installed names. With #185/#186 landing cross-library search, the candidate list becomes the agent's primary navigation instrument, so its signal-to-noise directly bounds stage-4 success.

issues.title: feat(agent): allow multiple tool calls per turn for CLI providers
issues.body:
### The problem

CLI providers (`claude-code`, `cursor`) talk to the model through the text tool protocol in [`src/agent/providers/tool-protocol.ts`](src/agent/providers/tool-protocol.ts). That protocol currently instructs the model to reply with **exactly one** JSON tool call per turn:

```text
To take an action, reply with EXACTLY ONE JSON object and nothing else
```

That conflicts with the system workflow in [`src/agent/prompts.ts`](src/agent/prompts.ts), which already tells the model that turns are scarce and independent calls should be batched in a single reply. The loop's 5-turns-remaining nudge says the same thing.

The parser (`parseToolCalls`) can already extract **multiple** brace-balanced JSON objects from one reply. The machine can batch; the protocol forbids it.

Net effect on Claude Code / Cursor runs:

- Exploration that needs several `read_file` / `search` / `record_constraint` / `resolve_affected` calls burns one turn each.
- Create stages and `do` runs hit the turn budget on serial tool use even when the work is independent.
- API providers (OpenAI / Anthropic native tool calling) already execute multiple tool calls in one turn, so CLI users pay a structural tax the keyed providers do not.

This is separate from conversation history trimming (#165 / PR #175): that reduces tokens per turn; this reduces the number of turns required for the same work.

### Proposed behavior

1. Change `renderToolProtocol` so CLI providers may emit **one or more** tool-call JSON objects in a single assistant reply (still preferably in fenced `json` blocks, still catalog-gated).
2. Keep `parseToolCalls`'s multi-object extraction as the source of truth; update the protocol text, malformed-call nudge, and any "exactly one" copy so they agree.
3. Align wording with the existing WORKFLOW batching rule and the convergence nudge in [`src/agent/loop.ts`](src/agent/loop.ts) so the instructions no longer conflict.
4. Preserve today's dispatch order for a single turn's tool list (sequential is fine for v1). Do not weaken spec-gating: tools absent from `availableTools(ctx)` must still not dispatch.
5. Add offline unit tests covering: one call, several independent calls in one reply, mixed prose + multiple calls, and rejection of locked or hallucinated tool names.

Example of an allowed CLI reply after the change:

````markdown
```json
{"tool": "read_file", "args": {"path": "docs/SPEC.md"}}
```

```json
{"tool": "read_file", "args": {"path": "docs/BOM.md"}}
```

```json
{"tool": "search", "args": {"pattern": "USB_DP"}}
```
````

All three should execute in the same turn, matching native multi-tool behavior on OpenAI/Anthropic.

### Alternatives you considered

- **Leave CLI on one-call-per-turn and only raise `maxTurns` / stage budgets.** That spends more budget on the same serial shape instead of fixing the protocol conflict. Related work like turn-budget escalation helps retries but does not remove the tax.
- **Rely on history trimming alone (#175).** Trimming lowers tokens per turn; it does not stop "one `read_file` = one turn."
- **Teach batching only in the prompt.** Already done; the protocol's "EXACTLY ONE" line undoes it for CLI providers.
- **Same-turn unlock of edit tools after `validate_change`.** Deliberately rejected elsewhere to keep the structural gate; out of scope here. This issue is only about allowing multiple already-advertised tools in one reply.

### Effect on the invariants

- **Spec-gated in:** no effect if catalog filtering stays. Edit/write tools remain absent from the advertised list until `validate_change` unlocks them; `dispatchTool` still re-checks.
- **Verification-gated out:** no effect. ERC/DRC/`finish` gates and the obligations ledger are unchanged. Batching may include `run_erc` with other calls in one turn; pass/fail semantics stay the same.

### Before submitting

- [x] I searched existing issues and the roadmap, and this is not already tracked as multi-tool CLI batching (history trim / turn-budget / stage quantization are adjacent but different).

issues.title: copperhead doctor reports ready even when the openspec CLI is missing, so the failure only surfaces mid-run
issues.body:
### The problem


Running `copperhead create` in an environment without the `openspec` CLI installed, `doctor` reports **ready**, all five of its checks pass: node, kicad-cli, git, provider, and project config. The actual failure only appears later, inside the `spec-seed` stage, when `validate_change` tries to shell out to `openspec` and fails. In my case this meant two separate real runs, roughly 70 minutes and 54.7k output tokens combined, spent before the actual root cause became clear, since the diagnosis surfaced as a runtime string rather than something `doctor` could have caught in under a second before any real work started.

**Confirmed directly from source, not assumed.** `runDoctor` at `doctor.ts:379-389` builds its check list from exactly five functions: `nodeCheck`, `kicadCheck`, `gitCheck`, `providerCheck`, and `projectCheck`, plus a conditional privacy check, nothing else. There is no `openspecCheck` function anywhere in the file, and `grep -i openspec src/commands/doctor.ts` returns zero matches. The file's own header comment describes its scope narrowly as *"a fast, LLM-free, network-free check of whether this machine can actually run a copperhead command."*

Worth noting this is also an **inconsistency with the project's own spec**, not just an omission. `SPEC.md` section 2.6 (Trigger mechanics) explicitly describes `openspec` as invoked *"as subprocess tools (same pattern as kicad-cli),"* treating the two as parallel external dependencies. But `doctor.ts` gives kicad-cli its own dedicated check, `kicadCheck`, while `openspec` has no equivalent, despite the spec grouping them together as the same category of dependency.

The actual `openspec` subprocess call lives in `src/openspec/cli.ts:16-27`, and returns a not-found error as a plain output string, `openspec CLI not found on PATH (npm i -g @fission-ai/openspec)`, not something `doctor` could surface early. That function is called from four sites, all at runtime, none of them a preflight:

- `openspecValidate` from `agent/tools.ts:199` (the `validate_change` tool handler), `commands/check.ts:57`, and `commands/sync.ts:120`
- `openspecArchive` from `agent/loop.ts:759`
- `openspecInit` from `commands/create.ts:665`

I also grepped `src/util/preflight.ts` and `commands/check.ts` specifically for any standalone openspec-availability check, none exists anywhere in the codebase.

This isn't hypothetical either. A fellow contributor and I hit genuinely different outcomes on the same PR branch purely because one of us happened to have `openspec` installed globally already, from an unrelated prior setup, and the other didn't. `doctor` gave no signal either way.

### Proposed behavior


Add an `openspec` presence check to `doctor`'s check list, alongside the existing five. An `openspecCheck` function, following the same pattern as `kicadCheck` or `gitCheck`, that attempts to resolve the `openspec` binary on PATH, or runs `openspec --version`, and reports a clear **FAIL** with the same install hint already embedded in `cli.ts`'s error string, `npm i -g @fission-ai/openspec`, rather than letting a user discover it only after a real run gets partway through `spec-seed`.

Given `create.ts` calls `openspecInit` directly during its own setup regardless of whether `openspec/config.yaml` exists yet, this check likely **shouldn't** be conditional on that file's presence the way the four runtime call sites are, since a fresh project won't have that file yet either, and would still hit the same wall on its first real run.

### Alternatives you considered


Leaving the check where it currently surfaces, inside `validate_change`'s error handling, and simply improving that error message. This would help marginally, but doesn't solve the core problem: a user has no way to know in advance, before spending real turns and tokens, that `spec-seed` is guaranteed to fail. A `doctor`-level check costs nothing to run and catches this before any real work begins.


### Effect on the invariants


**None.** This only adds a read-only diagnostic check to `doctor`, following the exact same pattern as the four checks already there. It doesn't touch spec-gating, verification-gating, or any mutation path.


### Before submitting

- [x] I searched existing issues and the roadmap, and this is not already tracked.

issues.title: check exits 0 when the configured schematic is missing, and says it is not configured
issues.body:
### What happened

`copperhead check` exits 0 when its schematic is configured but missing, and tells the user the schematic is not configured. Every check that depends on the schematic (ERC, drift, forbidden-pin constraints) is skipped together, and the result is reported as green.

Found by driving `runCheck` over fixture repos and varying the config.

### Reproduction

Config points at a schematic that does not exist, which is what a typo, a rename, or a moved file looks like:

```json
{ "docs": "docs/", "schematic": "hardware/board.kicad_sch", "board": "hardware/board.kicad_pcb" }
```

```
ok = true
erc: null   drc: null
drift.ok: true   openspec: null   constraints.ok: true
log:
  | ERC skipped (no schematic configured; run copperhead init)
  | DRC skipped (no board configured)
```

Two separate problems in that output.

**The gate passes.** [cli.ts](src/cli.ts) exits on `res.ok`:

```ts
process.exit(res.ok ? 0 : 1);
```

`ok` is computed with `??  true` for the skipped checks, so a repo where nothing was verified is indistinguishable from a repo that passed everything. In CI that is a green build. `create.ts` also calls `runCheck`, so the same result feeds the create flow.

**The message is wrong and points the wrong way.** [check.ts:33](src/commands/check.ts) says:

```
ERC skipped (no schematic configured; run copperhead init)
```

but the schematic *is* configured. The guard is `config.schematic && existsSync(...)`, and both arms produce the same message, so a missing file is reported as missing configuration. `copperhead init` is the wrong remedy: the fix is to correct the path or restore the file.

### Why this is worth separating from a plain "no schematic" repo

A repo with nothing configured reporting green is arguable, since there is genuinely nothing to check and `init` has not run. The case above is different: the repo was configured to be checked, and quietly stopped being checked. Nothing in the exit code or the message says so.

The contrast with the neighbouring failure mode is stark. With the schematic present but `kicad-cli` absent, the tool fails loudly and well:

```
KicadCliMissingError: kicad-cli not found on PATH
why it failed: copperhead verifies every mutation with kicad-cli ERC/DRC; ...
```

So the harmless case shouts and the dangerous case is silent.

### Scope

The same `config.schematic && existsSync(...)` guard appears three times in [check.ts](src/commands/check.ts) (lines 29, 45, 63) and twice in [sync.ts](src/commands/sync.ts) (lines 43, 133), so ERC, drift and the constraint check all skip together on the same condition.

### Suggested direction

Split the two conditions, and treat them differently:

- `config.schematic` unset: skip, and keep the current message and the green result.
- `config.schematic` set but the file missing: say so (`schematic configured at <path> but the file is missing`), and do not report `ok: true`. Either fail, or add a distinct not-verified state so CI can tell the difference.

I would rather not pick between "fail" and "new state" in a PR without a maintainer's view, since it changes what CI does for existing repos. Happy to send whichever you prefer, with the message fix either way.

### Version

`51bb26e` (main). Verified against `runCheck` directly; the with-schematic path needs `kicad-cli`, which I do not have on this machine, so I did not exercise the ERC/DRC success path.

issues.title: draft_schematic fails to find real chips that already exist in the stock KiCad library, under a different library file
issues.body:
## What happened

Running `create` end to end on a real board (ESP32 battery soil sensor, `examples/medium/esp32-soil-sensor.md`), `draft_schematic` reported four parts as "library not installed and not vendored":

- `TPS63900` (regulator)
- `TPS22860` (load switch)
- `SHT40` (humidity sensor)
- `FDC1004` (capacitance sensor)

The agent spent 30+ turns trying name variants, then correctly refused rather than guess a pinout, then burned a second full retry doing the same thing. Two separate runs hit `turn-budget-exhausted` on this alone.

## Root cause (confirmed against a real KiCad 10.0.5 install)

`resolveLibrarySymbol` (`src/kicad/symlib.ts:151`) and `SymbolSource.resolve` (`src/kicad/draft/symsource.ts:283`) both split a `lib_id` at the colon and open **only** the named library file (`findLibraryFile`, `symlib.ts:99`). If the part isn't in that one file, resolution fails, even when the part exists in the *stock* KiCad symbol set under a different library name.

Checked directly against the installed libraries, exact matches only:

| Chip | Guessed library | Actually lives in |
|---|---|---|
| SHT40 | `Sensor_Humidity` | `Sensor_Humidity` (right file, part is named `SHT4x` not `SHT40`) |
| TPS63900 | `Regulator_DCDC` | `Regulator_Switching` |
| FDC1004 | `Sensor` | `Sensor_Proximity` |
| TPS22860 | `Power_Switch` | not present anywhere in the stock set (closest is `TPS22810`, a different part) |

3 of the 4 were resolver failures, not missing parts: the tool never looked past the one file it guessed. The 4th (`TPS22860`) is a genuine gap, and is exactly the case Part 3 below is for.

## Proposed fix

**1. Cross-library, fuzzy search (fixes 3 of the 4 cases here).** When the guessed library file doesn't contain the part, search every discovered `.kicad_sym` file for a matching symbol before giving up: exact name match first, then a fuzzy/substring match (the same closest-candidate logic `resolveLibrarySymbol` already uses within one file, extended across all of them). Report the correct `lib_id` if found in exactly one place; report all candidates if ambiguous, so the agent (not the engine) decides — same "did you mean" pattern already used for typo'd names, just extended across files. Exact matches must be reported separately from fuzzy ones (confirmed by testing: a loose substring check alone would have wrongly suggested `TPS22810` as a match for `TPS22860`).

**2. When there's still no exact match anywhere, surface the closest fuzzy candidates as a possible substitute.** Rather than a bare failure, report the nearest names by similarity (already partially there via the closest-candidate list) so the agent can propose a substitute part, clearly labeled as unconfirmed rather than presented as the same chip.

**3. Let a project vendor its own extra libraries (for a genuinely absent part, like `TPS22860` here).** `SymbolSource` already accepts a `symbolDirs` override, but only as a test seam (`DraftOptions.symbolDirs`, `draft.ts:23`); it isn't reachable from `.copperhead/config.json`. Surfacing it as a real config option lets a project commit a manufacturer-provided or hand-authored `.kicad_sym` file and point the tool at it. No symbol content is authored automatically; a human supplies and reviews the file before it's used.

Auto-fetching a symbol from a third-party service with no human review was considered and set aside for now: it needs paid API access and would mean a design could ship with a symbol nobody checked, which is exactly the failure class this tool is built to prevent.

## Reproduction

```bash
copperhead create --repo <empty-repo> --brief examples/medium/esp32-soil-sensor.md
```

Stage 4 (schematic) hits the four failures above on a from-scratch build.

issues.title: sync verify: broken coverage path, and two matches that silently pass
issues.body:
### What happened

Differential-tested `syncVerify` in `src/commands/sync.ts` by driving it over fixture repos and varying one input at a time. Three defects, each reproduced against a control that shows the check working when the trigger is removed.

Reproduced on `51bb26e` by calling `syncVerify(repoRoot)` directly.

### 1. The coverage item builds a broken path when `docs` has no trailing slash

`src/commands/sync.ts:111` concatenates without a separator:

```ts
doc: `${config.docs}${name}`,
```

`DEFAULTS.docs` is `'docs/'`, so the default happens to work. `loadConfig` does not normalise the value though (`docs: raw.docs ?? DEFAULTS.docs`), so any config written without the trailing slash reports a path that does not exist:

```
docs: "docs"          ->  doc="docsDECISIONS.md"      doc="docsCHANGELOG.md"
docs: "docs/"         ->  doc="docs/DECISIONS.md"     doc="docs/CHANGELOG.md"   (correct)
docs: "docs/design"   ->  doc="docs/designDECISIONS.md"
```

The check itself is fine, since the existence test uses `path.join`. Only the reported location is wrong, which matters because the item's whole job is to tell you which file to create.

`path.posix.join(config.docs, name)` would fix it, matching how `docsDir` is built four lines earlier.

### 2. A budget is considered recorded when an unrelated key merely ends with its name

`src/commands/sync.ts:75`:

```ts
if (!Object.keys(registry).some((k) => k.endsWith(budget)))
```

`endsWith` matches on any suffix, not on a key segment, so an unrelated constraint silently satisfies the budget:

```
budget: cost=10, registry: { "power.unit_cost": ... }   ->  no dual-write item   (wrong)
budget: cost=10, registry: { }                          ->  reports it           (control)
```

`power.unit_cost` is a different quantity from a `cost` budget, but `"power.unit_cost".endsWith("cost")` is true, so the missing dual-write is never reported. Comparing the final dot-separated segment, `k.split('.').pop() === budget`, would match the intent, and is what the constraint branch above already does to derive `shortKey`.

### 3. The constraint dual-write audit matches short keys as bare substrings

`src/commands/sync.ts:65`:

```ts
const shortKey = key.split('.').pop()!;
if (docsText && !docsText.includes(shortKey))
```

`includes` is unanchored, so a short key is satisfied by any word that happens to contain it:

```
key "thermal.b", docs contain "the board has been built"  ->  no item   (wrong, 'b' is inside 'built')
key "thermal.b", docs contain "nothing here"              ->  reports   (control)
```

`b` is an extreme case, but the same holds for any short or common segment: a key ending `.vcc` is satisfied by `VCC_RAIL`, `.id` by `width`, and so on. It fails in the direction that hides work rather than creating noise, which makes it easy to miss.

This one overlaps #180, which proposes replacing the substring audit with deterministic reconciliation, so it may be better fixed there than patched here. Raising it with a reproduction anyway, since #180 describes the approach rather than the failure and the two fixes above are independent of it.

### Suggested direction

1 and 2 are small and self-contained. I am happy to send them as one PR with fixtures, and to leave 3 to #180 unless you would rather have a word-boundary match in the meantime.

### Version

`51bb26e` (main).

issues.title: check --fab documentation gate is never invoked: fab.ts has no callers
issues.body:
### What happened

`src/kicad/fab.ts` implements the documentation-presence gate for `check --fab`, and nothing calls it. The module is never imported, and the `--fab` flag it is written for does not exist yet.

Filing it separately from #181 because that one is a single dead obligation kind and this is a whole module, and the right answer here may well be "wire it up" rather than "delete it".

### The evidence

Every export has zero references outside its own file:

```
DRAFT_QUALITY_HEADING          used-elsewhere=0
CREATE_ORIGIN                  used-elsewhere=0
isCreateProducedRepo           used-elsewhere=0
draftQualitySection            used-elsewhere=0
isFilledDraftQuality           used-elsewhere=0
checkDocumentationPresence     used-elsewhere=0
```

The module itself is never imported:

```
$ grep -rn "kicad/fab" src/ --include="*.ts"
(no matches)
```

and there is no `--fab` flag anywhere in `src/`:

```
$ grep -rn -- "--fab" src/ --include="*.ts"
(no matches)
```

The only thing referencing any of it is `test/fab-docs.test.ts`, which is why it stays green.

### What is not running

`checkDocumentationPresence` is the entry point, and its docstring states the intent:

```
Documentation-presence check for `check --fab` (task 1.5):
- LAYOUT.md must have a filled `## Draft quality` section
- create-produced repos must also have DEVPLAN.md
```

Neither of those is enforced today. `isCreateProducedRepo` reads the `origin: "create"` marker that `copperhead create` writes into `.copperhead/config.json`, and that marker is set but never consulted for this purpose, so the "only create repos require DEVPLAN.md" distinction has no effect either way.

The logic looks finished rather than half-written: `isFilledDraftQuality` already treats an HTML comment or whitespace as unfilled, which is exactly the case `init` scaffolds, and the violations are already shaped in the drift-report voice with `claim: "release-ready"`. It reads like a gate that was built and tested ahead of the command that was going to call it.

### Suggested direction

1. **Wire it**, if `check --fab` is still planned: add the flag to `src/commands/check.ts`, load `LAYOUT.md` and the `devplanExists` / `isCreateRepo` inputs, and surface the violations the way the other checks do.
2. **Remove it**, if the fab gate moved elsewhere or was dropped, so the tests stop implying a check that does not run.

I would rather not guess which, since it depends on roadmap rather than code. Happy to send either once you say. If it is (1), one thing worth deciding at the same time: whether a missing `LAYOUT.md` should fail `--fab` on an init-only repo, since the current code always reports it, and only the DEVPLAN half is gated on `isCreateRepo`.

### Version

`51bb26e` (main). `fab.ts` last touched in #126.

issues.title: decision-log obligation can never be opened: onDecision() has no callers
issues.body:
### What happened

`decision-log` is a declared obligation kind whose only producer is never called, so it can never be opened. It is a sibling of the `constraint-dual-write` problem in #177, but the opposite failure: that one is opened and immediately cleared, this one is never opened at all.

Raising it separately because the fix is not the same, and because #177 is being cleaned up right now and it would be easy to wire this one up naively and create a permanent gate block.

### The evidence

`decision-log` appears in exactly three places, none of which is a call site:

```
src/agent/ledger.ts:11    | 'decision-log'          <- the type union
src/agent/ledger.ts:64    this.add('decision-log', summary, 'decision');
```

That `add` lives in `onDecision()`, and `onDecision` has no callers anywhere:

```
add                  src-callers=14  test-callers=2
clear                src-callers=9   test-callers=4
onConstraintChange   src-callers=1   test-callers=1
onDocEdit            src-callers=1   test-callers=1
onKicadEdit          src-callers=1   test-callers=5
onDecision           src-callers=0   test-callers=0     <-
```

It is the only hook on `ObligationsLedger` with none. There is also no `clear('decision-log', ...)` anywhere in `src/` or the tests.

### Why it looks like a missing wire rather than a spare kind

The tool that writes decisions exists and does everything except tell the ledger. `record_decision` in `src/agent/tools.ts` appends to `docs/DECISIONS.md` and marks the file touched, but never calls `ctx.ledger.onDecision(...)`:

```ts
await appendFile(p, entry + '\n', 'utf8');
ctx.decisions.push(`${decision} | why: ${rationale}`);
ctx.filesTouched.add(path.join(ctx.config.docs, 'DECISIONS.md'));
return 'decision recorded';
```

And `DECISIONS.md` is first-class memory elsewhere: `CLAUDE.md` lists it beside `CHANGELOG.md`, `docs-as-memory.md` calls it the append-only decision log, and `commands/sync.ts` checks both files by name.

### The trap for whoever fixes it

`changelog` is the closest working analogue, and it needs three pieces, not one:

```
ledger.ts:49     this.add('changelog', 'CHANGELOG.md entry for this run', file);   opened
loop.ts:690      ctx.ledger.clear('changelog');                                     cleared by the commit path
tools.ts:617     openObligations.filter((o) => o.kind !== 'changelog')              excluded from blocking
```

`decision-log` has none of the second or third. So calling `onDecision()` from `record_decision` without also adding a clear path would open an obligation that nothing can satisfy, and since the gate refuses while any obligation is open, the run could never reach `finish`. That is a worse failure than the current dead code.

### Suggested direction

Either:

1. **Remove it**, the same way #177 removes `constraint-dual-write`: drop the kind from the union and delete `onDecision`. Decisions are already recorded in `DECISIONS.md` and `ctx.decisions`, so nothing is lost.
2. **Wire it properly**, if a run that edits the design is meant to be forced to record a decision: call `onDecision` from `record_decision`, and clear it on the same commit path that clears `changelog`, or exclude it from `blocking` in the same way.

I lean towards (1) for now, matching #177: the invariant "every run must log a decision" is a policy question, and it should not arrive as a side effect of removing dead code. Happy to send either as a PR.

### Version

`51bb26e` (main).

issues.title: Implement constraint registry reconciliation in check_drift
issues.body:
## The problem

The `constraint-dual-write` obligation was originally intended to ensure that every documented constraint also existed in `.copperhead/constraints.json`. However, it was event-based and could not actually enforce that invariant. The obligation was opened and immediately cleared within `record_constraint`, making it unreachable by the commit gate (see #177).

Removing the dead obligation fixes the immediate bug, but it also leaves the `SPEC.md` portion of the existing dual-write audit relying on simple substring matching instead of deterministic reconciliation.

The Phase 1 design already places this verification in the deterministic verify phase of `copperhead sync` as the dual-write audit ("constraints.json vs doc/spec mentions in both directions"). The current implementation checks constraints documented in `docs/SPEC.md` by searching for constraint names as plain substrings, which can both miss inconsistencies and report false positives.

## Proposed behavior

Strengthen the existing dual-write audit performed during `copperhead sync` for constraints documented in `docs/SPEC.md`.

During verification:

- Parse the documented budgets from `docs/SPEC.md`.
- Read `.copperhead/constraints.json`.
- Perform deterministic reconciliation for `SPEC.md` budgets.
- Report inconsistencies when:
  - a documented budget is missing from the registry,
  - a registry constraint expected in `SPEC.md` is missing,
  - or both exist but their documented values disagree.

The existing heuristic for constraints documented outside `SPEC.md` remains unchanged. This keeps the change focused while strengthening the deterministic verification already described in the Phase 1 design.

## Alternatives you considered

Keeping the invariant in the sync-obligations ledger was considered, but the ledger only observes individual tool events.

A dual-write invariant depends on whether two artifacts agree after all edits have completed, making it a whole-state comparison rather than an event lifecycle. This is why the original implementation ended up opening and immediately clearing the obligation.

Replacing the existing dual-write audit with another event-based mechanism would recreate the same problem. Strengthening the existing deterministic verification for `SPEC.md` keeps the implementation aligned with the intended architecture while preserving the existing behavior for other documentation.

## Effect on the invariants

**Spec-gating:** No effect. This proposal does not change proposal validation or tool availability.

**Verification-gating:** Strengthens deterministic verification by ensuring `docs/SPEC.md` and `.copperhead/constraints.json` remain synchronized through the existing dual-write audit. It does not change ERC, DRC, repair, rollback, or any other verification behavior.

## Before submitting

- [x] I searched existing issues and the roadmap, and this is not already tracked.

issues.title: Reuse selected tscircuit ideas while preserving KiCad as source of truth
issues.body:
## Summary

Evaluate and implement selected ideas from the tscircuit ecosystem that improve Copperhead without adopting React/TSX or Circuit JSON as the design source of truth.

Copperhead must remain a verification-gated KiCad agent:

- `.kicad_sch` and `.kicad_pcb` remain authoritative.
- Existing KiCad files are modified only through anchored text replacement.
- Circuit JSON, if introduced later, may only be a derived read-only view.
- Every mutation remains subject to ERC, DRC where applicable, drift checks, and rollback protections.

## Motivation

tscircuit provides useful patterns for:

- AI-readable connectivity summaries
- JLCPCB/LCSC part discovery
- Supplier BOM and pick-and-place conventions
- Compact footprint descriptions
- EasyEDA/LCSC footprint retrieval
- KiCad import interoperability

Some of these capabilities fit Copperhead’s current architecture directly, while others require new safety and verification mechanisms.

## Current Copperhead state

The repository already has:

- Read-only schematic connectivity extraction through `listNets()` and `pinNets()`
- A human-facing `/nets` summary
- JLCPCB, DigiKey, and Mouser BOM export
- Optional LCSC columns in `BOM.md`
- `kicad-cli pcb export pos` usage as a board loadability probe
- A fully specified but unimplemented `add-part-research-tools` OpenSpec change

The repository does not currently have:

- An agent-facing pin-to-net summary
- JLCPCB CPL/pick-and-place export
- Runtime part-search tools
- Footprint generation or validation
- EasyEDA footprint retrieval
- Circuit JSON integration
- A tscircuit-exported KiCad fixture

## Proposed work

### 1. AI-readable connectivity summary

Create a shared deterministic connectivity summarizer from the existing KiCad parser.

- Group nets with attached refdes, pin numbers, and pin names
- Report unconnected pins explicitly
- Preserve sheet-local identity where required
- Reuse it in the REPL `/nets` command
- Expose it to the agent as a read-only `list_connections` tool
- Keep the existing `list_nets` tool for compatibility
- Do not inject the complete summary into every system prompt

Before exposing it to the agent, test junctions, unlabeled nets, power symbols, global and hierarchical labels, duplicate local labels across sheets, and explicitly unconnected pins.

The existing geometric parser must not be described as a complete KiCad netlister unless these cases are supported.

### 2. JLCPCB assembly export

Extend the completed supplier BOM export with deterministic placement export.

- Finish the relevant read-only fab-gate work: board footprint enumeration, schematic/PCB refdes and footprint parity, and BOM readiness
- Wrap `kicad-cli pcb export pos`
- Normalize output to JLCPCB CPL columns
- Add `copperhead export assembly --supplier jlcpcb`
- Produce a paired JLCPCB BOM and CPL
- Define units, coordinate origin, side names, and rotation conventions
- Add golden tests covering top/bottom parts, rotations, exclusions, and missing boards
- Add the paired output to create stage 6 after the standalone command is proven

### 3. tscircuit KiCad interoperability fixture

Add a provenance-marked project exported from tscircuit and verify that it works with:

- `copperhead init`
- `copperhead check`
- The readable connectivity summary
- JLCPCB assembly export

This is import compatibility, not a new tscircuit or Circuit JSON source format.

### 4. JLC/LCSC-first part research

Revise the existing `add-part-research-tools` OpenSpec change before implementation.

- Introduce provider-specific credential requirements
- Make the public `jlcsearch` provider keyless when `research.enabled` is true
- Keep Nexar, Brave search, and datasheet fetching as later milestones
- Normalize LCSC number, manufacturer part number, package, stock, pricing, and basic/extended catalogue status
- Cache selected results as `sourcing.<refdes>` constraints
- Dual-write MPN and LCSC information into `BOM.md`
- Validate cached sourcing snapshots offline in `check`
- Keep all live network activity behind one allowlisted, transcript-logged egress module
- Use recorded API fixtures in CI

The existing supplier export must remain network-free and consume only cached `BOM.md` data.

## Deferred work

The following are intentionally excluded from the initial implementation:

- React/TSX as a design format
- Circuit JSON as an edit representation
- Whole-file KiCad serialization
- Compact footprint DSL and `.kicad_mod` generation
- EasyEDA/LCSC footprint geometry retrieval
- Rich Circuit JSON viewers
- Autorouting or freerouting integration

Footprint generation requires a separate design because Copperhead currently refuses new KiCad files through `write_file`, has no `.kicad_mod` generator, cannot validate standalone footprint files, and must preserve its anchored-edit invariant.

## OpenSpec work

Create or update focused changes:

- `add-readable-connectivity`
- `add-jlcpcb-assembly-export`
- `add-part-research-tools`

Before changing the network safety rail, sync or archive `build-copperhead-phase-1` so the part-research safety delta modifies requirements present in the main specification.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The agent can request a deterministic net-to-pin summary without reading raw schematic text.
- [ ] `/nets` and the agent tool share one connectivity implementation.
- [ ] Existing `list_nets` behavior remains compatible.
- [ ] JLCPCB assembly export produces a matched BOM and CPL.
- [ ] Assembly export is deterministic, LLM-free, and network-free.
- [ ] A tscircuit-exported KiCad fixture passes the supported Copperhead workflow.
- [ ] JLC part search uses the structurally restricted research network boundary.
- [ ] Selected LCSC and sourcing data are cached in BOM/constraints.
- [ ] `check` validates sourcing snapshots without network access.
- [ ] KiCad remains the only mutation target and source of truth.
- [ ] No Circuit JSON or KiCad serializer enters the mutation path.
- [ ] Relevant OpenSpec changes validate.
- [ ] Typecheck, offline tests, and build pass.

## Verification

For each focused change:

```bash
openspec validate <change>
npm run typecheck
npm test
npm run build
```

Live supplier/API checks must remain opt-in and must be reported separately from the offline test suite.

## Upstream references

- https://github.com/tscircuit/jlcsearch
- https://github.com/tscircuit/circuit-json-to-readable-netlist
- https://github.com/tscircuit/footprinter
- https://github.com/tscircuit/easyeda-converter

issues.title: constraint-dual-write obligation is never observable because it is immediately cleared
issues.body:
### What happened

## Summary

`record_constraint` opens a `constraint-dual-write` obligation, but immediately clears it in the same function. As a result, the obligation is never observable by the commit gate and cannot enforce the intended same-turn dual-write invariant.

## Current behavior

Today `record_constraint` performs the following sequence:

```text
saveConstraint(...)
↓
ledger.onConstraintChange(...)
↓
ledger.clear("constraint-dual-write", key)
```

`onConstraintChange()` opens the obligation:

```ts
this.add("constraint-dual-write", constraintKey, constraintKey);
```

but it is immediately removed before the tool returns.

The commit gate therefore never sees an open `constraint-dual-write` obligation, so this invariant is never enforced.

## Why this matters

The design documents describe the constraint registry as a same-turn dual-write mechanism where every constraint should exist both in the documentation and in `.copperhead/constraints.json`.

However, the current implementation cannot enforce this because the obligation never survives long enough to reach the commit gate.

## Additional context

The existing `ledger.onDocEdit(file)` hook only receives the edited filename and does not know which constraint(s) were satisfied by that edit. Because of this, simply moving the `clear()` call is not sufficient. The obligation lifecycle likely needs to be redesigned, or the dead obligation should be removed if this invariant is no longer intended.

### Relevant locations

- `src/agent/ledger.ts` – `onConstraintChange()` opens the `constraint-dual-write` obligation.
- `src/agent/tools.ts` – `record_constraint` immediately clears the same obligation after opening it.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Inspect `record_constraint` in `src/agent/tools.ts`.
2. Observe that it calls `ctx.ledger.onConstraintChange(key, openNow)`.
3. Immediately afterwards, it calls `ctx.ledger.clear("constraint-dual-write", key)`.
4. Inspect `ObligationsLedger.onConstraintChange()` in `src/agent/ledger.ts` and observe that it adds the `constraint-dual-write` obligation.
5. Since the obligation is cleared in the same function, the commit gate never observes it as open.

### Output

```shell
No runtime error is produced.

The implementation opens a `constraint-dual-write` obligation and immediately clears it, making the obligation effectively unreachable by the commit gate and preventing enforcement of the intended dual-write invariant.
```

### Which command

create

### Model backend

Not Applicable

### copperhead version

0.9.0

### Node, KiCad, and OS

node v22.14.0, kiCad 10.0.5, windows 10

### Before submitting

- [x] I searched existing issues and this is not a duplicate.
- [x] I removed API keys and other secrets from everything I pasted.

issues.title: Verification gate: DC power-integrity checks via Ki-PIDA, extending the planned SPICE/openEMS checker surface
issues.body:
### The problem

Right now verification is purely structural — ERC, DRC, and drift checks confirm a board is wired up correctly and doesn't break any geometric rules, but none of them ask whether the board actually works as a piece of electronics. ROADMAP.md already has ngspice queued up as an optional gate for analog behavior (Phase 2, item 4), and SPEC.md already name-drops openEMS as a future checker for EMC, so this isn't a new category of work — it's a gap in a category the project has already committed to caring about. DC power integrity is the obvious next piece missing from that list: nothing today would catch an IR-drop violation, a current-density hotspot, or a power rail whose dependency chain is quietly broken.

A board can sail through ERC and DRC clean and still brown out a rail under real load, and right now copperhead has no way of knowing that happened. Closing this gap fits the tool's actual pitch — "nothing is done until the tools agree" — instead of stretching that pitch into something new. It's the same shape of problem SPICE and openEMS are already meant to solve, just further down the list.

### Proposed behavior

Add Ki-PIDA as a new verification tool, built the same way ERC and DRC already work, and opt-in the same way the planned SPICE gate is meant to be:

- A `run_power_integrity` tool, same shape as `run_erc`/`run_drc` (() → {violations: [...]}), that drives Ki-PIDA through KiCad's IPC-based Python Scripting API (KiCad 9.0+) to check IR/voltage drop, current density, thermal hotspots, and multi-rail dependency chains against whatever budgets are already sitting in SPEC.md and `.copperhead/constraints.json`.
- Opt-in, not default — same as the SPICE gate is planned to be. Nothing about a normal `copperhead check` run changes unless someone turns this on.
- Same repair-or-rollback behavior as everything else: a violation gets read back to the agent, it gets a shot at fixing it (adjusting a value, adding a pour, resequencing a rail) within the usual `maxRepairCycles` budget, and if that doesn't work the run rolls back and reports the violation exactly the way an ERC failure does today.
- Lives in the same places the other checks already live — `copperhead check --power` (or a config flag) on its own, the same `--json` violation format, and eventually folded into `copperhead check --fab` once that lands as one more thing a board has to clear before fab.

What it'd actually look like:

    $ copperhead check --power
    ERC ✓  DRC ✓  power-integrity ✗
    Violation: 3V3 rail — IR drop 0.19V exceeds 0.15V budget at U4 (constraints.json: power.rail_drop_max_V)
    1 violation, 0 warnings

### Alternatives you considered

- An RL-driven or physics-optimizing layout/routing engine — worth saying plainly that this isn't that, and shouldn't turn into that. SPEC.md and ROADMAP.md both say outright that copperhead isn't an autorouter and isn't trying to compete with tools like Quilter; SPEC.md even frames those tools as the thing copperhead's draft output is supposed to hand off to. This issue stays a checker, full stop — it never touches placement or routing.
- Folding this into the existing SPICE-gate roadmap item instead of filing separately: thought about it, but SPICE and Ki-PIDA aren't checking the same thing — one's transient/AC analog behavior, the other's DC power delivery — and they don't even share a scripting interface. Filing this as its own thing, but explicitly next to that item, not on top of it.
- openEMS instead of, or alongside, Ki-PIDA: also already on the roadmap (SPEC.md §8), and probably a good follow-up issue, but it's a different physics problem entirely (EM field simulation vs. DC power) with its own dependency on Gerber export. Left out here so this stays reviewable as one checker at a time.

### Effect on the invariants

Spec-gating: doesn't touch it. This is a new verification tool, not a write tool, so it has nothing to do with when edit tools unlock.

Verification-gating: makes it stricter, not looser, and only for repos that opt in. ERC and DRC don't change at all. Turn Ki-PIDA on and you've got one more thing a mutation has to clear before it's accepted, using the same repair-or-rollback path everything else already uses.
